mainTopic: נזקי בור: the ten-טפחים rule, the dispute between רב and שמואל over הבל and חבטה, and רב נחמן's ruling on an ox that fell into a shallow channel.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a short aggadic point: the plural ארך אפים shows that God is patient with both צדיקים and רשעים. A ברייתא then forbids clearing stones from your field into רשות הרבים. It tells of a man who mocked a חסיד's warning and later tripped on his own stones after he sold his field. A new משנה follows: anyone who digs a pit, ditch, cave, trenches or channels in public is liable, and the word בור teaches that a hole must be ten טפחים deep to count as deadly. Below ten טפחים, the digger is פטור if the animal dies but חייב if it is only injured. In the גמרא, רב says a בור makes the digger liable only for its deadly air (הבל), while שמואל says it also makes him liable for the impact (חבטה). Their practical difference is a mound in public, and each reads the word ״וְנָפַל״ his own way. The גמרא defends רב against challenges from the משנה. It explains why every kind of hole is listed, and it concludes that a shallow hole has enough air to injure but not to kill. Finally, רב נחמן declares an ox that fell into a shallow channel a טריפה, and רבא challenges him from the same משנה.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק say ״אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם״ in the plural?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק uses the plural form ארך אפים rather than the singular ארך אף.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says ״אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם״ (long-suffering, in the plural). Why doesn't it just say ״אֶרֶךְ אַף״ (singular)?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices an odd plural word in the description of God's patience and asks why it is there. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אפים is literally 'faces' or 'angers' in the plural. A single word would have been enough, so the גמרא assumes the plural form is teaching something extra.

phrases.english: 'Long-suffering' (literally 'long of angers'):
and it is not written 'long of anger' in the singular?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier aggadic discussion about God's patience, which began before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the plural form אפים come to teach?

steps.title: God is patient with both the righteous and the wicked
steps.stepSummary: The plural teaches two kinds of patience: toward צדיקים and toward רשעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is patient with the righteous and with the wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the plural form points to two groups. God is slow to punish both the righteous and the wicked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two 'angers' match two audiences. Even a צדיק's small sins are not punished right away, and a רשע is also given time to do תשובה.
steps.whatToRemember: God's patience does not mean He overlooks sin. It means He delays punishment for everyone, righteous and wicked alike.

phrases.english: Long-suffering toward the righteous and toward the wicked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the plural form.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The plural shows two kinds of patience, for צדיקים and for רשעים.

steps.title: Do not clear stones from your property into the public road
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a person should not throw stones from his own land into רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: A person should not clear stones from his own property into the public domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with a new rule: you may not clear your field by dumping its stones onto the public road.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Stones in a public place can trip people and animals, which ties into the theme of public hazards. The ברייתא teaches this as a rule of proper behavior.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A person should not clear stones from his own property
into the public domain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about public hazards.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not throw stones from his own property into רשות הרבים.

steps.title: A חסיד warns the stone-thrower, and the man laughs
steps.stepSummary: A story: a חסיד asks a man why he throws stones from land that is not his into land that is his, and the man mocks him.
steps.simpleTranslation: It once happened that a man was clearing stones from his property into the public domain. A pious man found him and said: 'Empty one, why are you clearing stones from land that isn't yours into land that is yours?' The man laughed at him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא tells a story to show the rule in action. A חסיד gives a strange-sounding warning, and the man mocks it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חסיד turns things around: your private field is not really 'yours' for good, but the public road always stays yours to use. The man cannot see this because right now the field belongs to him.
steps.confusionAlert: The חסיד is not mixed up about who owns which land. He means that the private field can be lost, while the public road will always be there for this man to use.

phrases.english: There was an incident with a certain man
who was clearing stones from his property into the public domain,
and a certain pious man found him.
He said to him: Empty one,
why are you clearing stones
from a property that is not yours into a property that is yours?
He mocked him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the ברייתא's rule with a story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חסיד warns that a private field is temporary, while the public road is permanently yours to use.

steps.title: The man sells his field and trips on his own stones
steps.stepSummary: Later the man had to sell his field, stumbled on those same stones in the public road, and admitted the חסיד was right.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some time later he had to sell his field. He was walking in that same public road and tripped on those same stones. He said: That pious man spoke well when he asked me why I was clearing stones from land that is not mine into land that is mine.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the warning coming true. The man now understands what the חסיד meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the field was sold, it truly was 'not his', and the public road was the only place he could still walk. His own stones became a hazard to him, which proves the ברייתא's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He spoke well to me (he was right)

steps.whatToRemember: Never put hazards in רשות הרבים. The public space belongs to you more lastingly than your own private land.

phrases.english: Some days later he had to sell his field,
and he was walking in that same public domain,
and he stumbled on those same stones.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: יָפֶה אָמַר לִי אוֹתוֹ חָסִיד –
phrases.english: He said: That pious man spoke well to me:
Why are you clearing stones
from a property that is not yours into a property that is yours.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the story and confirms the חסיד's warning.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The man's own stones hurt him once the field was no longer his, showing the חסיד was right.

steps.title: One who digs a pit in public is liable
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: if someone digs a בור in רשות הרבים and an ox or donkey falls in, he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who digs a pit in the public domain, and an ox or a donkey fell into it, is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with the basic law of בור: the digger pays for an animal that falls into his pit in a public place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is one of the main categories of damage, נזקי בור. The digger is responsible because he created a hazard in a place where people and animals walk.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (marks the start of a משנה)

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who digs a pit in the public domain,
and an ox or a donkey fell into it,
is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה on נזקי בור.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Digging a בור in רשות הרבים makes the digger liable when an animal falls in.

steps.title: Any kind of hole counts, not just a round pit
steps.stepSummary: The משנה widens the law: a pit, ditch, cave, trenches or channels all make the digger liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the same whether one digs a pit, a ditch, a cave, trenches or channels: he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה teaches that the shape of the hole does not matter. Any kind of dug-out hazard falls under the law of בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word names a different shape: a round pit, a long narrow ditch, a covered cave, and different trenches. All of them carry the same liability.

phrases.english: It is the same whether one digs a pit, a ditch, or a cave,
trenches or channels:
he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands the basic law to every type of hole.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All types of dug-out holes fall under the liability of בור.

steps.title: Then why does the תורה say 'pit'?
steps.stepSummary: If every kind of hole counts, why does the פסוק specifically mention a בור?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does the פסוק say 'pit'?
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks why the תורה uses the word 'pit' if all holes are included. This sets up the lesson in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the rule covers every shape, the specific word בור must be teaching some other detail. The answer will be about how deep the hole must be.

phrases.english: If so, why is 'pit' stated?
phrases.notes: שמות 21:33: 'And if a man shall open a pit.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what the word בור adds once all holes are included.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does the specific word בור in the פסוק teach?

steps.title: A deadly hole is ten טפחים deep
steps.stepSummary: The word בור sets the standard: just as a pit deep enough to kill is ten טפחים, so too any hole counts for death only at ten טפחים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Just as a pit that is deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths, so too anything deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה answers that the word בור gives the measurement: a hole is deadly when it is ten טפחים deep.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בור is the model for every other hole. The shape can be anything, but to count as deep enough to kill, the hole needs ten טפחים, just like a standard pit.

phrases.aramaic: מָה בּוֹר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית –
phrases.english: Just as a pit that has enough depth to kill
is ten handbreadths,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית –
phrases.english: so too anything that has enough depth to kill
is ten handbreadths.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה בּוֹר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by deriving a depth standard from the word בור.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word בור teaches that ten טפחים is the depth that can kill, for every type of hole.
steps.whyThisMatters: The ten-טפחים measurement is the standard for liability for death in all of נזקי בור.

steps.title: Below ten טפחים: exempt for death, liable for injury
steps.stepSummary: If the hole is less than ten טפחים and the animal dies, the digger is פטור. If the animal is only injured, he is חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they were less than ten handbreadths, and an ox or a donkey fell in and died, he is exempt. But if it was injured there, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the ten-טפחים rule. A shallow hole does not make the digger pay for a death, but he still pays for an injury.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A hole under ten טפחים is not considered deep enough to kill, so a death is not blamed on the digger. It can still cause injury, so the hole remains a בור for injuries. This is an exception in how the law is applied, not a removal of the category.
steps.whatToRemember: Ten טפחים or more makes the digger liable for death. Less than ten makes him liable only for injury.
steps.confusionAlert: A shallow hole still counts as a בור. The digger is only exempt for death, not for injury.

phrases.english: If they were less than ten handbreadths,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וּמֵת –
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died,
he is exempt.
But if it was injured in it, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ten-טפחים standard to shallower holes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Below ten טפחים, the digger is פטור for death but חייב for injury.

steps.title: רב: The pit makes him liable for its fumes, not its impact
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that the liability of בור is only for the הבל, not the חבטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: רב says: The pit the תורה made a person liable for is liable because of its fumes, not because of the impact of falling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting רב, who defines exactly what kind of damage a בור is blamed for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal that falls into a pit can be hurt in two ways: the hit when it lands, and the bad air at the bottom. רב says the תורה holds the digger responsible only for the bad air. The hit of landing does not count against him.

keyTerms.meaning: The hot, stuffy, deadly air at the bottom of a pit
The impact or hit when the animal lands
The תורה made a person liable

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rav says:
The pit for which the Torah made one liable
is for its fumes, and not for its impact.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: בּוֹר שֶׁחִיְּיבָה עָלָיו תּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא now asks what exactly the דין of בור from the משנה is based on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liability for בור is for the הבל only, not for the חבטה.

steps.title: Why רב holds this: the ground causes the impact
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רב: the impact comes from the ground itself, which the digger does not own.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems רב holds that, for the impact, it is the ground of the world that hurts the animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind רב's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The digger only made a hole. The ground at the bottom was always there, and it is the ground that hits the animal. So the hit is not really caused by the digger's pit, and only the bad air counts against him.

keyTerms.meaning: The natural ground, which belongs to no one in particular

phrases.english: Apparently he holds:
the impact — it is the ground of the world
that damages it.
phrases.notes: The ground at the bottom isn't something the digger made; he only took away the dirt above it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רב's ruling in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חבטה is caused by the natural ground, not by the digger.

steps.title: שמואל: Liable for the fumes, and even more so for the impact
steps.stepSummary: שמואל disagrees and makes the digger liable for both the הבל and the חבטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And שמואל says: He is liable for its fumes, and all the more so for its impact.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings שמואל, who disagrees with רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל agrees the הבל counts. But he adds the חבטה too, and calls it the more obvious case (״כל שכן״). For him, the hit of landing is plainly the pit's damage.

phrases.english: And Shmuel says:
For its fumes, and all the more so for its impact.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second opinion that argues with רב.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The digger is liable for both the הבל and the חבטה.

steps.title: שמואל's proof: even a pit full of wool sponges
steps.stepSummary: שמואל proves the הבל counts: the תורה makes him liable for any pit, even one where there is no impact.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say the תורה spoke only about the impact and not the fumes, I answer: the תורה spoke about a pit in general, even a pit full of wool sponges.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל heads off a possible objection and proves that the הבל alone is enough to make the digger liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think only the hit counts. But the תורה says ״בור″ with no conditions, so even a pit padded with soft wool, where the landing does not hurt, is included. In that pit, the only thing that can kill is the הבל, so the הבל must count.

phrases.english: And if you say:
The Torah spoke of its impact, and not of its fumes —
the Torah testified about the pit in general,
and even one full of wool sponges.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם תֹּאמַר: לַחֲבָטוֹ אָמְרָה תּוֹרָה, וְלֹא לְהֶבְלוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports שמואל's view that the הבל counts, so both causes are included.
steps.raayaObject: That the הבל alone makes the digger liable.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The תורה says ״בור״ with no conditions, which includes a pit padded with wool sponges.

steps.title: What is the practical difference between רב and שמואל?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks when רב and שמואל would actually rule differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question that sets up the next step: in what real case would רב and שמואל disagree?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a normal pit, an animal gets both the hit and the bad air, so both opinions make the digger liable. The גמרא wants a case where the result actually changes.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the two opinions just quoted differ in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case where רב and שמואל would rule differently.

steps.title: The difference: a mound built in a public area
steps.stepSummary: If someone builds a mound in רשות הרבים and an animal falls off it, רב says he is not liable and שמואל says he is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference is where someone made a mound in רשות הרבים. According to רב, he is not liable for a mound. According to שמואל, he is liable for a mound too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a case: a raised mound instead of a hole.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal that falls off a mound lands on open ground, so there is no bad air, only a hit. רב counts only the הבל, so he says the builder is not liable. שמואל counts the חבטה, so he says the builder is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, an area open to everyone

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up: here nothing was dug at all. The animal falls DOWN off a raised spot, so there is no bad air, only a hit.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them
where he made a mound in the public domain;
according to Rav — for a mound he is not liable,
according to Shmuel — for a mound he is also liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A mound in רשות הרבים: no הבל, only חבטה. רב says not liable; שמואל says liable.

steps.title: What is רב's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב exempts the builder of a mound.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רב's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind רב's ruling about the mound. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying the ground causes the hit is a logical claim. Now the גמרא wants to know where in the פסוק רב finds that a mound is not included.

phrases.english: What is Rav's reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of רב's side of the difference in step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the פסוק for רב's exemption of a mound.

steps.title: רב: ״וְנָפַל״ means a normal fall into something
steps.stepSummary: רב reads ״וְנָפַל״ as a normal fall down into a pit, which rules out falling off a mound.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the פסוק says ״וְנָפַל״, which means the digger is liable only when the animal falls in the normal way of falling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רב's source: the word ״וְנָפַל״ in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, ״וְנָפַל״ describes the usual kind of fall: walking along and dropping down into a hole. An animal that climbs up onto a mound and then falls off it does not fall in that normal way, so the builder is not liable.

keyTerms.meaning: "And it falls" (from the פסוק about בור)

phrases.english: Because the verse says: "And it falls" —
meaning only when it falls in the normal way of falling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17 by giving רב's source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״וְנָפַל״ requires a normal fall, which excludes falling off a mound.

steps.title: שמואל: ״וְנָפַל״ includes any fall
steps.stepSummary: שמואל reads ״וְנָפַל״ broadly, so falling off a mound is included.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to שמואל, ״וְנָפַל״ means any kind of fall at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives שמואל's reading of the same word, which closes this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions rest on the same word. שמואל does not limit ״וְנָפַל״ to a normal fall into a hole, so an animal falling off a mound also counts, and the builder is liable.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: liability for בור is only for the הבל, and ״וְנָפַל״ means a normal fall, so a mound is not included. שמואל: both the הבל and the חבטה count, and ״וְנָפַל״ means any fall, so a mound is included.

phrases.english: And according to Shmuel, "and it falls"
means any kind of fall at all.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives שמואל's reading of the same word, in contrast to רב.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ״וְנָפַל״ includes every kind of fall, so falling off a mound also makes the builder liable.

steps.title: Challenge to רב: what does the phrase 'so too, any' add?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה uses ״אַף כֹּל״ to extend the ten-טפחים rule beyond a בור. For שמואל, this includes a height. For רב, who exempts a fall from a height, the phrase seems to add nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: Why does the תורה say 'pit'? To teach that just as a pit deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths, so too anything deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths. That fits שמואל well, because 'so too, anything' includes a height. But according to רב, what does 'so too, anything' include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings our משנה to challenge רב. The extra words ״אַף כֹּל״ in the משנה seem to have no job in רב's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's phrase ״אַף כֹּל״ is meant to include something beyond a plain pit. For שמואל, it easily includes a fall from a height of ten טפחים, such as a mound. רב exempts the mound case, so the גמרא asks what extra case the phrase could be including for him.

keyTerms.meaning: Ten handbreadths, the depth a pit needs to be able to kill
So too, anything (a phrase that includes more cases)

phrases.english: We learned: If so, why does it say 'pit'?
phrases.notes: This line is quoted from our own משנה. The פסוק is שמות 21:33.

phrases.aramaic: מָה בּוֹר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית – עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים,
phrases.english: Just as a pit that is deep enough to kill is ten handbreadths,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כְּדֵי לְהָמִית – עֲשָׂרָה טְפָחִים.
phrases.english: so too, anything that is enough to kill is ten handbreadths.
This makes sense for שמואל: 'so too, anything' comes to include a height.
phrases.notes: A height is the mound case from Step 16, where the animal falls off it.

phrases.english: But according to רב, what does 'so too, anything' come to include?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רב's narrow reading of ״וְנָפַל״ against the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב, who exempts a person who builds a mound
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The extra phrase ״אַף כֹּל״ should include something. In רב's view, the most obvious candidate, a height, is excluded, so the phrase looks useless.

steps.title: For רב, the phrase includes trenches and channels
steps.stepSummary: According to רב, ״אַף כֹּל״ comes to include חריצין and נעיצין.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include trenches and water channels.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. The phrase ״אַף כֹּל״ includes other kinds of dug-out holes, not heights.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, the extra phrase still has a job. It extends the ten-טפחים rule to other holes in the ground, such as trenches and channels. It does not extend it to a fall off a raised mound.

phrases.english: To include trenches and water channels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge against רב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the phrase a different job
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In רב's view, ״אַף כֹּל״ had nothing left to include.
steps.terutzMaskana: It includes other kinds of holes, namely trenches and channels.

steps.title: But the משנה already names trenches and channels
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that חריצין and נעיצין are listed openly in the משנה, so ״אַף כֹּל״ should not be needed to include them.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the משנה teaches trenches and channels openly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. Why would the משנה need a hint to include something it already names?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's list already mentions חריצין and נעיצין by name. So the phrase ״אַף כֹּל״ still seems to add nothing new for רב.

phrases.english: Trenches and channels are taught openly in the משנה!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that ״אַף כֹּל״ includes trenches and channels
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Something that is already stated openly does not need to be included through an extra phrase.

steps.title: The משנה first states the law, then explains its source
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists the cases first, and then ״אַף כֹּל״ explains where in the תורה that law comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches them, and then explains.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the phrase is not repeating anything. It shows the source for the cases the משנה already listed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The listing of חריצין and נעיצין gives the law. The ״מָה בּוֹר... אַף כֹּל״ part explains how we learn that law from the תורה's word ״בּוֹר״. So רב's explanation of the משנה stands.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רב, ״אַף כֹּל״ gives the תורה source for trenches and channels, which the משנה already listed. It does not include a fall from a height.

phrases.english: It teaches the law, and then explains it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection in Step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The repetition has a different purpose
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Naming the cases twice is pointless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first mention gives the law, and the second gives its source.

steps.title: Why does the משנה list so many kinds of holes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the משנה needs to list every kind of hole separately.
steps.simpleTranslation: And all these cases that the משנה teaches, why do I need them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. Why not just say 'a pit' and stop there? This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists בור, שיח, מערה, חריצין and נעיצין. The גמרא wants to know what each one adds that the others do not.

phrases.english: And all these that it teaches, why do I need them?
phrases.notes: These are the different holes listed in the משנה: pit, ditch, cave, trenches and channels.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mentioning trenches and channels leads to a broader question about the whole list.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why each type of hole needs to be stated separately

steps.title: A pit alone would not teach the law for a long ditch
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה said only בור, we might think ten טפחים kills only because a pit is narrow and round, which traps deadly air. A long שיח might not trap that air.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed. If it taught only a pit, I would say that a ten-handbreadth pit has deadly fumes because it is narrow and round. But a ditch is long, so I might say that at ten handbreadths it has no deadly fumes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה needs to mention a שיח in addition to a בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pit kills partly because of the stale, deadly air trapped inside it, the הבלא. A narrow, round pit traps that air. A long ditch lets the air spread out, so we might think ten טפחים is not deadly there. The משנה tells us it is.

keyTerms.meaning: Deadly fumes or stale air in a pit

phrases.english: It is needed. For if it had taught only a pit,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: בּוֹר עֲשָׂרָה – הוּא דְּאִית בֵּיהּ הַבְלָא,
phrases.english: I would have said: it is a ten-handbreadth pit that has deadly fumes,
because it is narrow and round.
But a ditch, which is long,
I might say: at ten handbreadths it has no deadly fumes.

steps.triggerLanguage: צְרִיכָא; דְּאִי תְּנָא בּוֹר, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering why each case is needed.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A שיח is needed, because a long ditch might not hold deadly fumes the way a narrow pit does.

steps.title: A ditch alone would not teach the law for a wide cave
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה said only שיח, we might think it is deadly because it is narrow. A wide, rectangular מערה might not hold deadly air at ten טפחים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it taught only a ditch, I would say that a ten-handbreadth ditch has deadly fumes because it is narrow. But a cave is rectangular, so I might say that at ten handbreadths it has no deadly fumes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues and explains why the משנה must also mention a מערה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ditch is long, but it is still narrow, so it can trap deadly air. A cave is wide in every direction, so we might think its air is not deadly at ten טפחים. The משנה teaches that the same ten-טפחים rule applies to a cave too.
steps.whatToRemember: Every hole in the משנה's list is needed. Without each one, we might have thought its shape lets the deadly air escape, so it would not count as deadly at ten טפחים.

phrases.english: And if it had taught a ditch,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא: שִׁיחַ עֲשָׂרָה הוּא דְּאִית בֵּיהּ הַבְלָא,
phrases.english: I would have said: it is a ten-handbreadth ditch that has deadly fumes,
because it is narrow.
But a cave, which is rectangular,
I might say: at ten handbreadths it has no deadly fumes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the explanation of why each case is needed, moving from ditch to cave.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A מערה is needed, because a wide cave might not hold deadly fumes the way a narrow ditch does.

steps.title: Why the משנה also needs to list trenches after a cave
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה listed only a מערה, we might think its ten-טפחים fumes come from it being covered. Uncovered חריצין might not hold deadly fumes.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה had taught only 'cave,' I would have thought a ten-טפחים cave has deadly fumes because it is covered. Trenches are open on top, so I might think a ten-טפחים trench has no deadly fumes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps answering why the משנה lists every kind of hole. Now it explains why חריצין are needed after a מערה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מערה has a roof, so you might think its covering is what traps the deadly air. חריצין are open on top, so a learner could think air escapes and ten טפחים is not deadly. Listing חריצין shows that ten טפחים is deadly even without a covering.

keyTerms.meaning: A cave: a hole with a roof over it
Fumes or stale air inside a hole, which can kill
'I would have said': a mistaken first thought

phrases.english: And if it had taught 'cave,'
I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: מְעָרָה בַּעֲשָׂרָה הוּא דְּאִית בַּהּ הַבְלָא,
phrases.english: it is a cave of ten that has deadly fumes,
because it is covered;
but trenches, which are not covered,
say: at ten they have no deadly fumes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the chain from steps 25-26, moving from מערה to חריצין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why must the משנה list חריצין after מערה?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without it, we might think only a covered hole traps deadly fumes at ten טפחים.

steps.title: Why the משנה also needs to list channels after trenches
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה listed only חריצין, we might think their fumes come from straight walls that are no wider at the top. נעיצין open wider at the top, so the משנה must teach that they are deadly at ten too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה had taught only 'trenches,' I would have thought a ten-טפחים trench has deadly fumes because it is no wider at the top than at the bottom. Channels are wider at the top than at the bottom, so I might think a ten-טפחים channel has no deadly fumes. So the משנה teaches us that it does.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last link in the chain. The גמרא explains why נעיצין are needed after חריצין, then closes with קא משמע לן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חריצין have straight walls, so the air stays trapped. נעיצין slope outward and open wider at the top, so you might think the air escapes. The משנה lists them to show that ten טפחים is deadly even in that shape.

keyTerms.meaning: Channels: ditches that slope and get wider toward the top
'It teaches us': this is the new point the text is making

steps.whatToRemember: Every kind of hole in the משנה rules out a mistaken idea: round בור, then long שיח, then covered מערה, then open חריצין, then wide-topped נעיצין. At ten טפחים, all of them count as deadly.

phrases.english: And if it had taught 'trenches,'
I would have said:

phrases.aramaic: חֲרִיצִין עֲשָׂרָה הוּא דְּאִית בְּהוּ הַבְלָא,
phrases.english: it is trenches of ten that have deadly fumes,
because they are not wider
at the top more than at the bottom;
but channels,
which are wider at the top than at the bottom,
say: at ten they have no deadly fumes;
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the chain begun in step 25 with the last item, נעיצין.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why must the משנה list נעיצין after חריצין?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Without it, we might think a hole that is wider at the top lets the fumes escape and is not deadly at ten טפחים.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה: under ten exempt for death, liable for injury
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says a hole under ten טפחים is exempt if the animal dies but liable if it is injured. The גמרא suggests this shows the reason is lack of impact (חבטה), not lack of fumes.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: if the holes were less than ten טפחים deep, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, the digger is exempt. If it was injured, he is liable. Why is he exempt when it fell in and died? Isn't it because a hole that shallow doesn't have a deadly impact?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה to challenge the view that a pit kills through its fumes (הבלא). It suggests the exemption under ten is about the fall (חבטה).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Below ten טפחים the animal can be injured but not killed. The גמרא suggests the fumes are there even in a shallow hole, so the only thing missing must be a strong enough fall. If so, a fatal pit kills through חבטה, and that challenges the fumes view.

keyTerms.meaning: 'We learned' in a משנה: introduces a quote
The impact or blow of falling and hitting the bottom
Exempt, does not have to pay

steps.confusionAlert: Even though this line is phrased as a question ('Isn't it because...?'), it is really an attack on the view that a pit kills through its fumes.

phrases.english: We learned in the משנה:
If they were less than ten handbreadths,

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וָמֵת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.
And if it was injured in it, he is liable.

phrases.aramaic: נָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וּמֵת – פָּטוּר;
phrases.english: 'An ox or donkey fell into it and died: exempt';
what is the reason?
Is it not because it has no deadly impact?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the list of holes to a new challenge drawn from the משנה's rule about holes under ten טפחים.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's view (step 11) that liability for a בור is only for its fumes (הבל), not its impact (חבטה).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The exemption for death below ten seems to come from a weak fall, which suggests death in a pit is caused by חבטה.

steps.title: No: a shallow hole is exempt because it lacks deadly fumes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a hole under ten is exempt because it has no deadly fumes, not because of the impact.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. He is exempt because the hole has no deadly fumes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the fumes view. It reads the משנה's exemption below ten as a lack of הבלא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The suggestion was that a shallow hole lacks a deadly fall. The answer reverses it: a shallow hole lacks deadly air. So the משנה fits the view that a pit kills through fumes.

phrases.english: No, it is because it has no deadly fumes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the reason behind the משנה's ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under ten is exempt because there is no deadly impact.
steps.terutzMaskana: Under ten is exempt because there are no deadly fumes.

steps.title: But if there are no fumes, why is he liable for injury?
steps.stepSummary: If a shallow hole has no fumes, why does the משנה make the digger liable when the animal is injured?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why is he liable if the animal is injured? It has no fumes!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. If a pit's harm comes from fumes and a shallow hole has none, it should not cause any damage at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the fumes view, the fumes are what make a pit dangerous. Saying a shallow hole has no fumes seems to leave no reason for liability on injuries. Yet the משנה says the digger is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: 'If so': if we accept your answer

phrases.english: If so,
why is he liable if it was injured in it?
But it has no fumes!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אִם הוּזַּק בּוֹ חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 30 that a hole under ten has no fumes.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No fumes should mean no harm, yet the משנה makes him liable for injury.

steps.title: Enough fumes to injure, not enough to kill
steps.stepSummary: A shallow hole has some fumes: enough to cause damage, but not enough to cause death.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: there are not enough fumes to kill, but there are enough fumes to injure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the problem by splitting how strong the fumes are. This settles the challenge from the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 30's 'no fumes' really means no deadly fumes. Below ten טפחים, the air is weak but still harmful. That explains both rulings: exempt for death and liable for injury.
steps.whatToRemember: Under ten טפחים, the fumes can injure but cannot kill. That is why the digger pays for injury but not for death, and the fumes view still stands.

phrases.english: They answer:
there are no fumes for death,
but there are fumes for damages.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 31 and refines the answer of step 30.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A shallow hole has no fumes at all, so it should not injure.
steps.terutzMaskana: A shallow hole has weak fumes: enough to injure, not enough to kill.

steps.title: An ox falls into a water channel and רב נחמן declares it a טריפה
steps.stepSummary: An ox fell into a shallow irrigation channel. Its owner slaughtered it, and רב נחמן ruled it a טריפה.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was once an ox that fell into a water channel. Its owner slaughtered it, and רב נחמן declared it a טריפה (forbidden to eat).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic by telling a real-life story. An ox fell into a shallow ditch and was slaughtered, and רב נחמן forbade the meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner was afraid the ox would die from the fall, so he slaughtered it quickly to save the meat. רב נחמן worried that the fall had crushed the ox's insides, which makes it a טריפה. The channel was shallow, less than ten טפחים, and that detail drives the rest of the discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: A water channel dug for irrigating fields; a fairly shallow ditch
He declared it a טְרֵפָה, an animal with a fatal injury that is forbidden to eat even after שְׁחִיטָה

phrases.english: There was a certain ox that fell into a water channel,
phrases.notes: This is a ditch for watering fields. It was shallow, less than ten טפחים deep, and that detail matters later.

phrases.english: its owner slaughtered it.
Rav Naḥman declared it a tereifa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion. The previous steps asked whether a hole under ten טפחים has fumes; this story raises the related question of whether such a fall has impact.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An ox slaughtered right after falling into a shallow channel is a טריפה.

steps.title: Had the owner waited a day, the ox would have been kosher
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says the owner should have bought some flour for food and learned the הלכה: if the animal survives twenty-four hours after the fall, it is kosher.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: If the owner of this ox had taken a קב of flour, and gone and learned in the study hall that if the animal survives twenty-four hours it is kosher, he would not have lost his ox, which was worth many קבין of flour.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן adds a practical lesson to the story. The owner rushed to slaughter the ox; if he had waited a full day, the ox would have been permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal that falls and is slaughtered right away may be a טריפה because of possible crushing. If it lives for twenty-four hours, we know it was not badly hurt, and it is kosher. The owner traded an expensive ox for the cost of one small bag of flour.

keyTerms.meaning: A קַב of flour; a small amount of food

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the הלכה for an animal that fell: if it survives a full day, it is permitted.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said:
If the owner of this ox had taken
a kav of flour,
phrases.notes: He means: eat bread for a day instead of rushing to eat the ox's meat.

phrases.english: and gone and learned in the study hall:
if it survived twenty-four hours, it is kosher;
he would not have lost the ox
that is worth several kav.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: אִי שְׁקֵיל מָרֵיהּ דְּהַאי תּוֹרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב נחמן comments on the story and adds the rule that surviving twenty-four hours makes a fallen animal kosher.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fallen animal that survives twenty-four hours is kosher.

steps.title: רב נחמן holds that a fall under ten טפחים has impact
steps.stepSummary: From רב נחמן's ruling, the גמרא infers that he holds a fall of less than ten טפחים can still cause a damaging impact.
steps.simpleTranslation: So it seems that רב נחמן holds that there is impact even in a fall of less than ten טפחים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion about what רב נחמן must believe. This sets up the challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The channel was less than ten טפחים deep, yet רב נחמן worried that the ox's organs were crushed. That means he holds that even a short fall can have a real חבטה. This position will clash with how the next step reads the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: The impact of a fall, the blow when hitting the ground

phrases.english: Apparently, Rav Naḥman holds:
there is impact in less than ten handbreadths.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out the principle behind רב נחמן's ruling in the story.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רב נחמן holds that a fall of less than ten טפחים can cause a dangerous impact.

steps.title: רבא challenges רב נחמן from the משנה about shallow holes
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes the משנה: if a hole is less than ten טפחים deep and an animal dies in it, the digger is exempt. He argues that the reason must be that a shallow fall has no impact.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא challenged רב נחמן: The משנה says that if the holes were less than ten טפחים deep, and an ox or donkey fell in and died, the digger is exempt. What is the reason? Is it not because a fall that short has no impact?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's view using our משנה. If a shallow hole had real impact, why would the digger be exempt when the animal dies?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads the משנה's exemption as proof that a fall under ten טפחים has no חבטה. That contradicts רב נחמן, who made the ox a טריפה because of impact from a shallow fall. Back in steps 29–30 the גמרא explained this same line as being about missing fumes (הבל), not impact. רבא is now pressing the impact reading against רב נחמן.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him from an authoritative source
Is it not because…? (a leading question that pushes an answer)

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same line of the משנה the גמרא already discussed in steps 29–32. There the issue was whether the reason is lack of impact or lack of fumes. Here רבא uses the impact reading as a weapon against רב נחמן.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection to Rav Naḥman:
If they were less than ten handbreadths deep,
phrases.notes: This quotes our משנה. 'They' means the different kinds of holes listed there.

phrases.aramaic: וְנָפַל לְתוֹכוֹ שׁוֹר אוֹ חֲמוֹר, וּמֵת – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and an ox or a donkey fell into it and died, he is exempt.
What is the reason?
Is it not because it has no impact?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the principle inferred in step 35 using the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's view that a fall of less than ten טפחים has impact (חבטה)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה exempts the digger when an animal dies in a hole under ten טפחים. The natural reason is that such a fall has no impact, which contradicts רב נחמן's ruling that the ox was a טריפה from a shallow fall.
